title: Personal pronouns
explain_md:
German has **three words for "you"**. That is the only hard part.

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| **1st** | ich · I | wir · we |
| **2nd informal** | du · you | ihr · you all |
| **3rd** | er / sie / es | sie · they |
| **formal** | Sie · you | Sie · you |

**du** — friends, family, children, students.
**ihr** — more than one of the above.
**Sie** — strangers, officials, shops, anyone older you don't know. Always capitalised.

Get **Sie** wrong and you sound rude. Get **du** wrong and you sound stiff. When unsure, use **Sie** and wait to be offered *du*.

drills.q: Talking to your new flatmate, same age:
drills.why: Same age, living together — informal du.

drills.q: Asking a police officer for directions:
drills.why: A stranger in an official role always gets Sie.

drills.q: Asking two friends if they're coming:
drills.why: More than one person, both informal — ihr.

title: sein — to be
explain_md:
**sein** is irregular in every language, and German is no exception. Learn it as six sounds, not as a rule.

```
ich   bin      wir  sind
du    bist     ihr  seid
er    ist      sie  sind
            Sie  sind
```

Notice **wir / sie / Sie all take `sind`** — three of the six forms are the same word. There are really only four to memorise: *bin, bist, ist, seid*.

drills.why: ihr → seid (the one that catches everyone)

title: The alphabet, and spelling out loud
explain_md:
Same 26 letters as English, four extra characters, and about eight names that will catch you out.

| letter | sounds like | letter | sounds like |
|---|---|---|---|
| **e** | *ay* | **i** | *ee* |
| **a** | *ah* | **j** | *yot* |
| **v** | *fow* | **w** | *vay* |
| **y** | *üpsilon* | **z** | *tset* |

The trap is **e** and **i**: German **e** sounds like English *A*, and German **i** sounds like English *E*. Spelling your email address is where this bites.

**ä ö ü** are said *A-Umlaut, O-Umlaut, U-Umlaut*, or just *ä, ö, ü*.
**ß** is *Eszett* or *scharfes S*. It is never capitalised at the start of a word, and you may always write **ss** instead.

On the phone, Germans spell with names — *A wie Anton, B wie Berta*. You do not need the list, but you need to recognise what is happening when somebody does it at you.

drills.q: German **e** is pronounced like the English letter…
drills.why: German e sounds like English A. This is the one that ruins spelled-out email addresses.
Eszett, or scharfes S. It looks like a Greek beta and is not one.

drills.q: You did not catch a name. You say:
drills.why: Asking someone to spell it is the fastest repair in the language.

title: haben — to have
explain_md:
**haben** is almost regular. Only *du* and *er/sie/es* drop the **b**.

```
ich   habe     wir  haben
du    hast     ihr  habt
er    hat      sie  haben
            Sie  haben
```

So: **hast** and **hat** are the two to watch. Everything else keeps the *b*.

title: Present tense — regular verbs
explain_md:
Take the infinitive, chop off **-en**, add the ending. That is the whole system.

```
wohnen  →  wohn-  +  ending

ich   wohn e      wir  wohn en
du    wohn st     ihr  wohn t
er    wohn t      sie  wohn en
```

Five endings: **-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en**.

One wrinkle: if the stem ends in **-t** or **-d** (*arbeiten*, *finden*), you insert an **-e-** so it's pronounceable → *du arbeit**e**st*, *er arbeit**e**t*.

drills.why: stem ends in -t, so insert -e-: arbeitet

title: der, die, das
explain_md:
Every German noun has a gender. It is **not** logical — *das Mädchen* (girl) is neuter. Learn the article **with** the noun, never the noun alone.

| | definite | indefinite |
|---|---|---|
| masculine | **der** Mann | **ein** Mann |
| feminine | **die** Frau | **eine** Frau |
| neuter | **das** Kind | **ein** Kind |
| plural | **die** Kinder | — |

Note **der** and **das** share *ein* — the indefinite article makes no masculine/neuter distinction here.

Some patterns that hold most of the time:
- **-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion** → always **die**
- **-chen, -lein** → always **das**
- **-er** (person doing something) → usually **der**

drills.why: -chen is always neuter, regardless of meaning.

title: The verb goes second
explain_md:
This is the rule that makes German sound German. **The conjugated verb is always the second element** in a statement — not the second *word*, the second *block*.

```
  1            2        rest
[Ich]        [wohne]   in Berlin.
[Heute]      [wohne]   ich in Berlin.
[Seit 2024]  [wohne]   ich in Berlin.
```

Move anything to the front and the subject jumps **behind** the verb. English doesn't do this — *"Today I live"* stays put, German flips to *"Heute wohne ich"*.

This is the single most common mistake English speakers make, for years.

drills.why: Heute is slot 1, verb bin is slot 2, then the subject.
Verb must be second — subject moves behind it.
"In Berlin" is one block = slot 1, so wohne is slot 2.
Same flip after any fronted element.

title: Asking questions
explain_md:
Two kinds, both simple.

**W-questions** — question word first, verb second (the same slot-2 rule):
```
Woher   kommst   du?
Wo      wohnst   du?
Was     machst   du?
```

**Yes/no questions** — just put the verb **first**:
```
Kommst  du aus Indien?
Wohnst  du hier?
Hast    du Zeit?
```

No *do/does* helper verb. German has nothing equivalent — *"Do you live here?"* is simply *"Wohnst du hier?"*

drills.why: woher = from where. wo = where, wohin = to where.
Verb goes first in a yes/no question.

title: nicht vs kein
explain_md:
Two ways to say no, and picking the wrong one is a classic beginner tell.

**kein** negates a noun that has *ein* or no article:
```
Ich habe ein Auto.   →  Ich habe kein Auto.
Ich habe Zeit.       →  Ich habe keine Zeit.
```

**nicht** negates everything else — verbs, adjectives, and nouns with *der/die/das* or a possessive:
```
Ich arbeite.         →  Ich arbeite nicht.
Das ist gut.         →  Das ist nicht gut.
Ich kenne den Mann.  →  Ich kenne den Mann nicht.
```

Quick test: **could you say "a" or "any" in English?** Then it's *kein*.

drills.why: Kaffee is a bare noun → kein (accusative masculine → keinen).

title: Accusative — the object case
explain_md:
When a noun is the **object** of the sentence — the thing being acted on — masculine articles change. **Only masculine.**

| | subject (nom.) | object (acc.) |
|---|---|---|
| masc | **der** / **ein** Mann | **den** / **einen** Mann |
| fem | **die** / **eine** Frau | **die** / **eine** Frau |
| neut | **das** / **ein** Kind | **das** / **ein** Kind |
| plural | **die** Kinder | **die** Kinder |

```
Der Mann  →  Ich sehe  den Mann.
Ein Apfel →  Ich esse  einen Apfel.
Die Frau  →  Ich sehe  die Frau.     (unchanged)
Das Kind  →  Ich sehe  das Kind.     (unchanged)
```

So three quarters of the table does nothing. **Learn der → den and ein → einen and you have accusative.**

drills.why: Hund is masculine and it's the object → einen.

title: Numbers, and why they run backwards
explain_md:
Above twenty, German says the **units before the tens**.

**einundzwanzig** — literally *one-and-twenty*.
**vierundsechzig** — *four-and-sixty*, 64.

Written as one word, however long. *siebenundachtzig* is 87.

This is not a curiosity. A price, a house number or a platform is said at full speed and you will hear the small digit first — **zweiundvierzig** starts with *zwei* and means 42, not 24. Listening for the ending is the skill.

Two spellings worth knowing: **sechzehn** and **siebzehn** drop a letter (not *sechszehn*, not *siebenzehn*), and **dreißig** is the only ten spelled with **ß**.

drills.why: vier-und-zwanzig — four and twenty. The small digit is said first.
zwei-und-fünfzig. The ending fünfzig is what tells you it is in the fifties.
sechzehn loses the s. So does siebzehn.

title: Modal verbs — können, müssen, wollen
explain_md:
Modal verbs express ability, obligation and desire. Two things to know:

**1. ich and er/sie/es are identical** — no ending on either.
```
ich   kann      wir  können
du    kannst    ihr  könnt
er    kann      sie  können
```

**2. The other verb goes to the very end, as an infinitive.**
```
Ich  kann   Deutsch  sprechen.
Ich  muss   heute    arbeiten.
Ich  will   nach Hause  gehen.
```

This is the *Satzklammer* — the sentence bracket. The modal is in slot 2, the real verb waits at the end. It feels strange at first and then becomes automatic.

| | means |
|---|---|
| können | can, be able to |
| müssen | must, have to |
| wollen | want to |
| möchten | would like (polite) |
| dürfen | be allowed to |

drills.why: The infinitive goes to the very end.

title: Telling the time, and the halb trap
explain_md:
**halb drei is half past TWO.**

German counts *towards* the coming hour. *halb drei* means half way to three. Every English speaker gets this wrong once, usually while missing something.

| clock | German |
|---|---|
| 2:00 | zwei Uhr |
| 2:15 | viertel nach zwei |
| 2:30 | **halb drei** |
| 2:45 | viertel vor drei |
| 2:10 | zehn nach zwei |
| 2:50 | zehn vor drei |

**Two systems, both alive.** In conversation people use the twelve-hour form above. Timetables, appointments and anything official use the 24-hour clock read straight out: *vierzehn Uhr dreißig* for 14:30.

When an Amt or a doctor gives you a time, you will hear the official form. When a friend does, you will hear *halb*. Learn to answer both with *Um wie viel Uhr?*

examples.de: Der Termin ist um vierzehn Uhr dreißig.
Um wie viel Uhr beginnt das?

drills.why: Half way TO seven, so 6:30. The single most expensive mistake in beginner German.

drills.q: The doctor says **um sechzehn Uhr**. That is…
drills.why: The 24-hour clock, read straight out. Official contexts always use it.

drills.q: It is 9:45. A friend would say…
drills.why: Quarter before ten. German looks forward to the next hour.

title: mein, dein, sein — possessives
explain_md:
Possessives take **exactly the same endings as *ein***. Learn *ein* and you already know all of them.

| | |
|---|---|
| mein | my |
| dein | your (du) |
| sein | his / its |
| ihr | her / their |
| unser | our |
| euer | your (ihr) |
| Ihr | your (formal) |

```
ein  Bruder   →  mein  Bruder      (masc, subject)
eine Schwester →  meine Schwester   (fem)
ein  Kind     →  mein  Kind        (neut)
     Eltern   →  meine Eltern      (plural takes -e)

Ich sehe einen Bruder → Ich sehe meinen Bruder   (masc object)
```

One trap: **ihr** means both *her* and *their*, and capitalised **Ihr** means *your (formal)*. Context decides.

title: am, um, im — when something happens
explain_md:
Three prepositions, chosen by the **kind** of time word. Learn them as a set; picking between them is not a judgement call.

| | for | example |
|---|---|---|
| **am** | days, parts of the day | am Montag, am Abend |
| **um** | clock times | um acht Uhr |
| **im** | months, seasons, years | im Januar, im Sommer |

Two exceptions worth knowing on day one:

**in der Nacht** — not *am*. The night is the odd one out.
**Am Wochenende** for the weekend as a whole.

And no preposition at all with **heute, morgen, gestern**: you say *morgen* and *heute Abend*, never *am morgen* for tomorrow.

examples.de: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.

drills.why: am for days of the week.
heute, morgen and gestern stand alone.

title: Making plurals
explain_md:
German has **five** plural patterns and no reliable way to predict which. Learn the plural with the word, like the article.

| ending | example | notes |
|---|---|---|
| **-e** | Tisch → Tisch**e** | often masculine |
| **-er** | Kind → Kind**er** | often adds umlaut: Haus → H**ä**us**er** |
| **-(e)n** | Frau → Frau**en** | almost all feminine nouns |
| **-s** | Auto → Auto**s** | loanwords |
| **— (none)** | Zimmer → Zimmer | often -er/-el/-en endings |

The one dependable rule: **nouns ending in -e take -n** (Woche → Wochen), and **almost every feminine noun takes -n or -en**.

The plural article is always **die**, whatever the gender.

title: ich möchte — the polite one
explain_md:
**ich möchte** is the most useful form a beginner owns. It means *I would like*, and it works in every shop, café and office in the country.

| | |
|---|---|
| ich **möchte** | wir **möchten** |
| du **möchtest** | ihr **möchtet** |
| er/sie/es **möchte** | sie/Sie **möchten** |

Note **ich möchte** and **er möchte** have no ending. That is not a typo — it is how this group of verbs behaves.

**Say möchte, not will.** *Ich will einen Kaffee* is grammatical and lands like *I want a coffee* said flatly to a stranger. Germans are direct, but not that direct in a shop.

A second verb, if there is one, goes to the **end**: *Ich möchte bezahlen.*

examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.
Would you like something to drink?
What would you like to eat?

drills.q: Ordering in a café, the natural choice is:
drills.why: möchte is the polite form. will is blunt to a stranger.
No ending in the ich form — like a modal verb.

drills.q: Where does the second verb go? Ich möchte …
drills.why: The infinitive goes last. This is the bracket that runs through all of German.

title: Adjectives after sein — the easy half
explain_md:
After **sein**, an adjective takes **no ending at all**. None. Whatever the gender, whatever the number.

*Der Tisch ist **groß**.*
*Die Lampe ist **groß**.*
*Das Fenster ist **groß**.*
*Die Fenster sind **groß**.*

One form, four sentences. This is the half of German adjectives that is easier than English.

**The other half is not, and it is not A1.** Put the adjective *before* the noun — *der große Tisch* — and it takes an ending that depends on gender, case and which article is in front of it. That is a B-level table and this course does not pretend otherwise.

So: describe things with **sein** and you can say almost anything. *Das Auto ist rot* rather than *das rote Auto*, until much later.

drills.why: After sein there is never an ending, whatever the gender.
Plural changes nothing. Still no ending after sein.
Predicative — after sein. The other two need adjective endings, which are not A1.
